title: The gluteal region: extensors above, rotators below
summary: One big extensor, two abductors that keep you level, and six short rotators guarding the sciatic nerve.
objectives: Name the superficial and deep gluteal muscles with their nerves
Explain the Trendelenburg sign in terms of the abductor mechanism
Justify the upper outer quadrant for an intramuscular injection
Distinguish hip extension against gravity from pelvic stabilisation during single-leg stance
takeaways: Gluteus maximus extends (inferior gluteal nerve); medius and minimus abduct and stabilise the pelvis (superior gluteal nerve).
The hip drops on the side opposite the weak abductors.
Piriformis is the key: everything else in the region is described as above or below it.
Rising from a chair strongly recruits hip extensors; single-leg pelvic control depends particularly on gluteus medius and minimus.

steps.title: The superficial three
steps.text:
Gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body, running from the ilium, sacrum and sacrotuberous ligament down to the iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity. It is a powerful extensor — but not of walking on the flat. It works for climbing stairs, rising from a chair and sprinting.

Under it lie gluteus medius and, deeper still, gluteus minimus, both fanning from the ilium to the greater trochanter. Tensor fasciae latae completes the group at the front, tightening the iliotibial tract.

check.q: Which everyday movement uses gluteus maximus hardest?
check.a: Rising from sitting, or climbing stairs — not level walking.

steps.title: The abductor mechanism
steps.text:
Stand on one leg. Gravity acts through the midline, well medial to the hip you are standing on, and would tip the pelvis down on the unsupported side. Gluteus medius and minimus of the standing side contract to hold it level.

Paralyse them — a superior gluteal nerve injury, or simply a painful hip — and the pelvis drops on the opposite side when the patient stands on the affected leg: a positive Trendelenburg sign. Walking becomes a lurch as the trunk swings over the weak hip to move the centre of gravity.

check.q: A patient stands on the right leg and the left side of the pelvis drops. Which muscles are weak, and on which side?
check.a: The right gluteus medius and minimus — the sign is named for the side that drops but the lesion is on the standing side.

steps.title: Piriformis, the landmark
steps.text:
Piriformis leaves the front of the sacrum, passes out through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the greater trochanter. It nearly fills that foramen, and everything else entering or leaving the gluteal region is described as passing above or below it.

Above: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels. Below: the inferior gluteal nerve and vessels, the pudendal nerve, the nerve to obturator internus, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve and the sciatic nerve.

check.q: Which structure leaves the pelvis above piriformis?
check.a: The superior gluteal nerve and vessels.

steps.title: The short external rotators
steps.text:
Below piriformis, running laterally to the trochanter, are superior gemellus, obturator internus, inferior gemellus and quadratus femoris, with obturator externus deep in front. Obturator internus makes a right-angled turn round the lesser sciatic notch, using the bone as a pulley.

Together they laterally rotate the hip and — more importantly — hold the head of the femur in the acetabulum, the way the rotator cuff holds the humeral head. They are the reason a fractured neck of femur leaves the leg externally rotated.

steps.title: Where to put the needle
steps.text:
The sciatic nerve emerges below piriformis and runs down midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter — that is, through the lower medial part of the buttock.

So an intramuscular injection goes into the upper outer quadrant, or better still into the ventrogluteal site over gluteus medius, with the palm on the greater trochanter and the fingers spread to the iliac crest. A misplaced injection is still a cause of iatrogenic foot drop.

check.q: Which quadrant of the buttock is safe for an intramuscular injection, and what are you avoiding?
check.a: The upper outer quadrant — avoiding the sciatic nerve, which runs through the lower medial part.

steps.title: Two everyday tasks ask different questions
steps.text:
Picture rising from a low chair. The trunk begins forward over flexed hips, and gluteus maximus helps extend those hips to bring the body upright. Hamstrings and other muscles assist, so this is a coordinated task rather than an isolated test of one muscle.

Now picture standing on one leg. The main new challenge is preventing the opposite side of the pelvis from dropping, which particularly loads gluteus medius and minimus on the standing side. Difficulty with both tasks can involve different parts of the gluteal group. Separate the demand for extension from the demand for control in the frontal plane.

check.q: Which demand chiefly distinguishes single-leg standing from simply extending the hip to rise from a chair?
check.a: Single-leg standing requires the supporting hip abductors to control the pelvis against a tendency to drop on the opposite side.

title: The three compartments of the thigh
summary: Front, back and inside — each with one nerve, one action and one clean story.
objectives: Name the muscles of each compartment and its nerve
Explain why the hamstrings are called that and what makes biceps femoris different
Describe the adductor canal and its contents
Relate the pes anserinus tendons to three different thigh compartments and nerves
takeaways: Anterior: quadriceps and sartorius, femoral nerve, extends the knee.
Medial: the adductors and gracilis, obturator nerve, adduct the hip.
Posterior: the hamstrings, tibial part of the sciatic nerve, extend the hip and flex the knee.
Sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus meet at the pes anserinus despite having femoral, obturator and tibial-division sciatic supply respectively.

steps.title: Three compartments, three nerves
steps.text:
The thigh divides cleanly. Anterior: femoral nerve, knee extension. Medial: obturator nerve, hip adduction. Posterior: sciatic nerve, hip extension and knee flexion.

Notice that each nerve corresponds to a different part of the lumbosacral plexus, which is why the compartments are a useful way to localise a nerve injury: a patient who cannot extend the knee has a femoral problem, one who cannot adduct has an obturator problem.

check.q: Which nerve supplies the adductor compartment?
check.a: The obturator nerve (with a contribution from the sciatic to part of adductor magnus).

steps.title: Quadriceps femoris
steps.text:
Four heads into one tendon and then into the patella and the tibial tuberosity. Rectus femoris comes from the pelvis and so also flexes the hip; the three vasti come from the femur and only extend the knee.

Vastus medialis deserves special attention: its lowest oblique fibres pull the patella medially and resist lateral dislocation. It is the first part of the quadriceps to waste after a knee injury, in days rather than weeks, and the last to recover.

check.q: Which head of quadriceps also flexes the hip, and why?
check.a: Rectus femoris — it arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine, so it crosses both joints.

steps.title: Sartorius and the adductor canal
steps.text:
Sartorius is the longest muscle in the body, running from the anterior superior iliac spine down and medially to the upper medial tibia. Its actions — flexing, abducting and laterally rotating the hip while flexing the knee — put the leg in the cross-legged tailor's position it is named for.

Its real importance is as a roof. Under its middle third lies the adductor canal, a triangular tunnel containing the femoral artery, femoral vein and saphenous nerve, running from the apex of the femoral triangle to the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus, where the vessels pass into the popliteal fossa.

check.q: What are the three contents of the adductor canal?
check.a: Femoral artery, femoral vein and the saphenous nerve.

steps.title: The adductor group
steps.text:
Adductor longus, brevis and magnus in three layers, with gracilis in front of them running all the way to the tibia and pectineus at the top.

Adductor magnus is the interesting one: it has an adductor part supplied by the obturator nerve and a hamstring part supplied by the sciatic — a muscle sitting on the boundary between two compartments, and a reminder that the divisions are developmental rather than absolute. The gap between its hamstring part and the femur is the adductor hiatus.
steps.pitfall: Gracilis is the only adductor to cross the knee, so it also flexes and medially rotates it.

steps.title: The hamstrings
steps.text:
Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally. All arise from the ischial tuberosity, all cross both hip and knee, and all are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve — except the short head of biceps femoris, which comes from the common fibular division and does not cross the hip.

Because they cross two joints they are stretched at both ends when you sprint with the hip flexed and the knee extending, which is exactly when they tear. Their tendons form the upper borders of the popliteal fossa.

check.q: Which hamstring is not supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve?
check.a: The short head of biceps femoris — common fibular division.

steps.title: Testing the three
steps.text:
Extend the knee against resistance: femoral nerve, L3–L4, and the same segments as the knee reflex. Squeeze the knees together: obturator, L2–L4. Bend the knee against resistance: sciatic, L5–S1.

Add sensation — anterior thigh femoral, medial thigh obturator, back of thigh posterior femoral cutaneous — and you can localise almost any thigh nerve lesion at the bedside without a single investigation.

check.q: The knee jerk tests which roots?
check.a: L3 and L4, through the femoral nerve.

steps.title: Three compartments meet on the medial tibia
steps.text:
The pes anserinus, or goose's foot, is the shared region of insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the proximal medial tibia. From anterior to posterior their tendons follow that same order.

Each tendon brings a different compartment to the same destination: sartorius from the anterior thigh through the femoral nerve, gracilis from the medial thigh through the obturator nerve, and semitendinosus from the posterior thigh through the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Together they assist knee flexion and medial rotation of a flexed leg, while retaining different actions at the hip.

check.q: Which three nerves reach the muscles that form the pes anserinus?
check.a: Femoral to sartorius, obturator to gracilis, and the tibial division of the sciatic to semitendinosus.

steps.mnemonic: Sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus: anterior to posterior at the goose's foot.

title: The four compartments of the leg
summary: Four boxes below the knee, four nerves, and the surgical emergency that comes from their being boxes.
objectives: Name the four compartments, their muscles, nerves and actions
Recognise the presentation of acute compartment syndrome
Trace the tendons behind the medial malleolus in order
Explain why tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior can produce the same inversion action from opposite compartments
takeaways: Anterior: dorsiflexors, deep fibular nerve. Lateral: everters, superficial fibular nerve. Superficial posterior: plantarflexors, tibial nerve. Deep posterior: invertors and toe flexors, tibial nerve.
Pain on passive stretch is the earliest reliable sign of compartment syndrome; pulses are the last thing to go.
Behind the medial malleolus: Tom, Dick and a Very Nervous Harry.
Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts; tibialis posterior plantarflexes and inverts. Their ankle actions differ but their inversion actions cooperate.

steps.title: Four boxes
steps.text:
The leg is wrapped in tough crural fascia and divided by the interosseous membrane and two intermuscular septa into four compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior and deep posterior.

Each has its own nerve and its own action, and — the point of the lesson — each is a closed space with almost no room to swell.

steps.title: Anterior: dorsiflexion, and the nerve that drops the foot
steps.text:
Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius, all supplied by the deep fibular nerve. They dorsiflex the ankle and extend the toes: the muscles that clear the foot in the swing phase of walking, and that lower it gently after heel strike.

Lose them and the foot slaps and drags — foot drop, with a high-stepping gait to clear the toes. The deep fibular nerve's only sensory territory is the small web between the first and second toes.

check.q: Where does the deep fibular nerve supply skin?
check.a: The web space between the first and second toes — a small but very specific patch.

steps.title: Lateral: eversion
steps.text:
Only two muscles: fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, supplied by the superficial fibular nerve. Both evert the foot and help plantarflex it.

Fibularis longus is remarkable: its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus, then crosses the entire sole obliquely to reach the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform. It therefore supports the transverse arch and presses the first ray down — which is what stops you rolling onto the outside of the foot.

check.q: Where does the tendon of fibularis longus insert?
check.a: The base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform, after crossing the sole.

steps.title: Superficial posterior: the calf
steps.text:
Gastrocnemius, with two heads from the femoral condyles, soleus from the tibia and fibula, and the vestigial plantaris. They join into the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, the thickest tendon in the body, and plantarflex the ankle with enormous power — they must lift the whole body weight at every step.

Because gastrocnemius crosses the knee it is stronger with the knee straight; soleus works whatever the knee is doing, and it is soleus that does the postural work of standing. Soleus is also the calf pump: its venous sinuses are emptied by walking, and the reason immobility causes deep vein thrombosis.
steps.clinical: Simmonds' test: squeeze the calf with the patient prone. No plantarflexion means a ruptured Achilles tendon.

steps.title: Deep posterior, and Tom Dick and Harry
steps.text:
Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and popliteus, supplied by the tibial nerve. Tibialis posterior inverts the foot and is the main dynamic support of the medial arch.

Their tendons pass behind the medial malleolus in a fixed order, front to back: Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery, tibial Nerve, flexor Hallucis longus — Tom, Dick and a Very Nervous Harry. Compression under the flexor retinaculum here is tarsal tunnel syndrome.
steps.mnemonic: Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry — front to back behind the medial malleolus.

check.q: Which structure lies between flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus behind the medial malleolus?
check.a: The posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve.

steps.title: Compartment syndrome
steps.text:
A closed fascial box plus bleeding or swelling equals rising pressure. When the pressure exceeds capillary perfusion pressure the muscle becomes ischaemic — and it does so long before the arterial pulse disappears, because the artery is a high-pressure vessel.

So do not wait for pulselessness. The earliest sign is pain out of proportion, and above all pain on passive stretch of the muscles in that compartment: passively dorsiflex the toes in a suspected deep posterior syndrome. The treatment is an urgent fasciotomy, and the anterior compartment of the leg is its commonest site in the body.

check.q: Which sign of compartment syndrome appears earliest?
check.a: Pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles. Pulselessness is a late and unreliable sign.

steps.title: Two tibialis muscles, one shared direction
steps.text:
Tibialis anterior passes in front of the ankle, so it dorsiflexes. Tibialis posterior passes behind the medial malleolus, so it plantarflexes. Both tendons approach the medial side of the foot, where their lines of pull help produce inversion.

The two muscles can therefore cooperate in one movement while opposing each other in another. The fibularis muscles on the lateral side provide the main opposing eversion pull. Rather than assigning a muscle one action only, trace which side of each joint axis its tendon crosses.

check.q: Why do tibialis anterior and posterior both invert even though one dorsiflexes and the other plantarflexes?
check.a: They pass on opposite sides of the ankle flexion axis but both pull towards the medial side of the foot.

title: The sole of the foot
summary: Four layers whose job is not to move the toes but to hold the foot together under load.
objectives: Name the four layers of the sole in order
Describe the plantar aponeurosis and its clinical importance
Give the territories of the medial and lateral plantar nerves
Distinguish the second-toe reference axis of toe abduction from the middle-finger axis in the hand
takeaways: Layer 1: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi.
The medial plantar nerve is the median nerve of the foot; the lateral plantar nerve is its ulnar nerve.
The intrinsic muscles act mostly as a stabilising sheet, contracting through the stance phase.
Toe abduction and adduction are described relative to the second toe; the corresponding reference in the hand is the middle finger.

steps.title: The plantar aponeurosis first
steps.text:
Before any muscle, a thick triangular sheet of fascia runs from the medial tubercle of the calcaneus forwards, splitting into five slips for the toes. It protects the sole, binds it together and — through the windlass mechanism — raises the arch as the toes extend.

Traction at its origin causes plantar fasciitis, and a chronic pull can produce a calcaneal spur, though the spur is a consequence rather than the cause of the pain.

steps.title: The four layers
steps.text:
Under the aponeurosis, four layers, superficial to deep.

One: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi. Two: the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus, with quadratus plantae and the lumbricals. Three: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis. Four: the interossei, with the tendons of tibialis posterior and fibularis longus crossing the sole.

check.q: Which three muscles make up the first layer of the sole?
check.a: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi.

steps.title: Quadratus plantae, the corrector
steps.text:
In the second layer, quadratus plantae runs from the calcaneus forwards to insert into the tendon of flexor digitorum longus.

Flexor digitorum longus enters the sole obliquely from the medial side, so if it pulled alone the toes would curl medially. Quadratus plantae pulls its tendon straight, converting an oblique pull into a straight one. It is a rare example of a muscle whose only job is to correct the line of action of another.

check.q: What does quadratus plantae actually do?
check.a: It straightens the oblique pull of flexor digitorum longus so the toes flex in line.

steps.title: Two nerves, one pattern you already know
steps.text:
The tibial nerve divides under the flexor retinaculum into medial and lateral plantar nerves, and they repeat the hand's arrangement.

The medial plantar nerve is the median nerve of the foot: it supplies the medial three and a half toes and only four muscles (abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical). The lateral plantar nerve is the ulnar nerve of the foot: the lateral one and a half toes and everything else.
steps.mnemonic: Medial plantar = median of the foot; lateral plantar = ulnar of the foot.

steps.title: What the intrinsics are really for
steps.text:
Individually these muscles are weak, and few people can move a single toe. Recorded together during walking, though, they fire through the whole stance phase.

They are a tensioning sheet: they stiffen the foot as load passes across it and act with the plantar fascia to control how much the arch flattens. Weakness of the intrinsics — in diabetic neuropathy, for instance — lets the toes claw and shifts pressure onto the metatarsal heads, which is where the ulcer then forms.
steps.clinical: Clawed toes plus loss of protective sensation is the anatomy of the diabetic foot ulcer, and it is why the metatarsal heads are checked at every review.

check.q: Why do the metatarsal heads ulcerate when the intrinsic muscles fail?
check.a: The toes claw, so load shifts from the toe pulps onto the metatarsal heads.

steps.title: The reference toe is the second
steps.text:
The dorsal interossei abduct the toes and the plantar interossei adduct them, but the reference axis is the second toe. The second toe can move to either side of that axis; the third, fourth and fifth are brought towards it by the plantar interossei.

The mnemonic DAB and PAD still works, but copying the middle-finger reference from the hand gives the wrong axis in the foot. Both groups also help flex the metatarsophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints through the toe expansions, contributing to stable contact with the ground.

check.q: Which toe defines the reference axis for toe abduction and adduction?
check.a: The second toe, rather than the third as in the hand's middle-finger reference.
